en: The sage Vācaspa said:
"You are Māyā, since the worlds have been conquered by you;
I am neither stainless nor invincible, for truth does not contradict falsehood."
O Goddess, you are stainless, yet [the world] is stained; let there be no further praise for this. "I have conquered," "I have been conquered"—in truth, this is merely a false affliction.
Śiva, the Goddess, and your own conduct have been truly understood by me as being one with the ultimate reality. || 27 ||
O Śaṅkara, that which illuminates everything truly appears as if it were real; however, O Goddess, this luminosity should be understood as [merely] conventional in your system. 28.
Just as fire is not perceived when joined with wood,
Śiva is likewise unmanifest; O Śivā, I am myself the light within this entire world.
"I am formless like space, or I possess form by my own will.
O Goddess, O Maheśvarā, this form which you bear is accomplished through your will. 30.
To you alone [belongs] that which is beautiful: the bearer of the crescent of the young moon;
a garland made of severed heads upon the head, a mass of matted locks, and here, serpents. 31.
His eye is a blazing fire; his earring is the Lord of Serpents;
his food is the terrible poison; his necklace is a corpse; his deer is a jackal;
his ointment is funeral ashes; and his bowl is a skull.
Our ornaments are serpents, our forms are various, and our garment is the hide of an elephant.
Our movement is in the great cremation ground, and an old donkey is our vehicle.
The hosts of spirits are our attendants; if we are destitute because of these, what of it? (34–35)
O ascetic at the foot of the banyan tree, you have attained a supreme form, seeing me with eyes filled with affection as I am endowed with every grace. (36)
If your form were to produce delight for the eyes, then you would surely lead the inhabitants of the great worlds, served by Brahmā and others, to that [state]. (37)

Then, that person like you— who has burnt away the pride of Darpaka (Kāma), who is victorious everywhere in the world, and who possesses neither shame nor self-importance— is beyond the reach of words. (38) (P.2a, F.2b, 1st line) For him, neither shame nor pride exists from any source whatsoever.
"O best of men, forgive all of that; may you be victorious. || 39 ||

Having spoken thus, the Mother of the worlds fell silent; her moon-like face was turned aside as she listened to his reply. Then the Lord of all beings, having offered a gentle smile, [spoke] once more to the living beings.
He laughed at Ambikā, his own non-differentiated Śakti, who was turned away from him. || 40 ||
O Śiva, on that day when the goddess Navadhūṛ does not exist, I too shall not be a creator;
nor shall there be pride or ego, for I abide everywhere like the sky. 41.
If this form, which is a source of joy to the eyes, is a means for your pleasure, then behold this manifested form with your eyes wide open to their ears. 42.
Having spoken thus to the daughter of the mountain, the mistress of all the worlds, Sūta [described] how she possessed unsurpassed beauty, such that her splendor did not possess any hardness. 43.
Tender with the exquisite beauty of a thousand billion Cupids, it shines like ten million suns and is as cooling as ten million moons. (5th line) 44.
With a face of gentle smile, a lotus-like countenance, and large, gracious eyes;
richly adorned with divine ornaments and garlands, and anointed with divine perfumes and unguents;
[she was] graced with noble necklaces, armlets, bracelets, bangles, and earrings.
Adorned with costly garments, he was girded with a belt of jewels and graced by many virtues.
Having washed away the dust from the eyes of the gods—even those who possess jeweled anklets, crowns, and forehead marks—it is worthy of their gaze. 47.
Her limbs are radiant with the entire quintessence of beauty, fit to be licked by the young cakora birds that are Gaurī’s eyes;
she is of uncreated form, stainless, and her feet are worthy of service.
The moon-crested Lord split the king of mountains like a lotus petal.
[Thus ends the second chapter in the Bhaktamāhātmya of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
Then Haimavatī, having beheld the most wonderful form of the Lord... 50.
Astonished and bowing, the Goddess propitiated the Supreme Lord, the God; [she said:
"Obeisance to Śiva, together with his attendants."
There, he joyfully beheld the beautiful peak of Kailāsa. || 79 ||
For the sake of service, he prostrated at the feet of the gods who were present there;
he kissed that skull resting on the hand of the Bull-riders,
and Śiva said again and again, "You are a hollow vessel."
(…) here he was nourished until maturity, becoming one who has mastered the scope of both the Vedas and the Vedāntas. || 81 ||
The Lord of the World recited the titles "Sundareśānubimba" and others, [and described] the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the worlds. 82.
And he taught Sundara the two paths of concealment and manifestation;
and on one occasion, to Sanaka and the others who were inquiring about their doubts, he imparted the beautiful determination regarding the Lord of bonds and those bound by them.
83. (4th line) He caused Sundara to attain the realization of the Lord of bonds and those bound by them.
What is the use of saying more in this matter? [He] abandoned Umā, the daughter of the mountain. || 84 ||
O Śambhu, he who is independent and beautiful shall become the possessor of all perfections.
(5th line) Then the gods and the Daityas, having come together, made a firm resolve. 85.
Desiring the nectar of immortality, they all churned the ocean of milk;
having made Mount Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope,
they squeezed out all medicinal herbs and cast them into the water.
While the great ocean was being churned with effort by the gods and the dānavas. || 87 ||
Unable to endure the crushing pressure of the mountain's arms, Vāsuki, mangled by wounds from sharp stones, gasped in pain. (88)
They vomited forth a terrible poison, a confluence of the defects of the waters, known as Hālāhala, resembling the fire of universal dissolution;
it became solidified, by which the three worlds were scorched. (89) (Line 8)
The Sindhu river, burning away the forests and mountains, [drank] the heavy poison of the Sindhu.
Like an unobstructed river flowing from this shore to the other, you [advanced];
by the force of the heat of the *hālāhala* poison, the gods and asuras were shattered. 91.
Even among the foremost beings of the worlds, not one was seen who could withstand him;
Rudra and Brahmā [fled] out of fear, and Hari turned black with distress. Even the wielder of the trident did not destroy his weapons, and the effort of the Destroyer to subdue him came to naught.
When the Lord of Treasures has departed, he is both unconscious and highly wise. 93.
Other gods and Daityas fainted on the bank of the Siddha-river;
likewise, the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, sages, and other sky-dwellers [fell]. 94.
Having heard of the violence of the Hālāhala poison, the Lord of Beings, the beautiful one, commanded Śiva, the bull-bannered god who is the refuge and protector, on Mount Kailāsa.
And he seized that terrible, full-blown [flower], which was as radiant as a jambu fruit, with the tip of his hand.
Beholding his beautiful hand, which was radiant with a dark-blue *hālāhala* poison,
the Lord showed it to the Daughter of the Mountain,
like a fully blossomed lotus surrounded by bees. 97.
And having given him the name Hālāhalasundara,
Hara took it from his hand; and by the command of the Lord of Elephants, he too drank it.
It became her ear-ornament. || 98 ||
Beholding Sundara, who had effortlessly removed the great burden of the beings dwelling in the three worlds,
they considered him to be Maheśvara himself manifest before their eyes.
[Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Deeds of Sundara," in the *Bhaktamāhātmya* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*.]
When Agastya, by the command of Maheśa, swallowed the great poison,
he then became beautiful, proud, and the foremost among the lords of the Gaṇas. 100.
Perceiving his arrogance, the All-Self, the Moon-crested Lord,
then formed the resolve to bestow upon him a complete instruction.
At that time, two female attendants were sent for the sake of Gaurī’s success.
Viśodhanenditā is one [deity] known by the name Kamalī... 102.
Both Ambikā and Śambhu, accompanied by Mṛḍānī, remained together in the Sundara garden as the trees were covered in blossoms.
Having perceived their deliberation, [he waited] until the end of the transformation of forms beneath the flowering trees.
Like lightning amidst dark clouds in the Mallikā garden of Gaurī. || 104 ||
His feet, possessing the luster of refined gold and clad in garments resembling *kiṃśuka* flowers, were as beautiful as land-lotuses and possessed well-formed soles. 105.
O King, your thighs shine like the quivers of the God of Love upon the ground dyed with lac, resembling the brilliance of a mountain peak of jewels;

your knees possess the splendor of the back of the king of tortoises, and your thighs are as beautiful as the Malaya mountains. 106. (2nd line) Your shanks are like the form of the quiver of the Mind-born God. Your knees have the beauty of the back of the lordly tortoise, and your broad thighs are like the Malaya range.
The golden plates were clearly visible, elevated by the uniform chanting [of prayers]. || 107 ||
Her girdle was struck by the wheels of the chariot of Love;
her beautiful waist, with its slightly loosened knot, was visible;
and the two lines of hair were perceived at the end of her hand as she reached toward her slender middle.
It possesses the excellence of the three folds [of the belly] and is radiant with a navel as deep as a lotus petal. 109.
Her breasts, firm and smooth, were swelling with milk; she was adorned with a long necklace, a cluster of flowers, and a cow’s udder-shaped ornament. 110.
Her sprout-like hands, variegated with clusters of blossoms in the form of jewel rings and bracelets, bore curved gems that were not harsh to the touch.
(Verse 112) He possesses two beautiful arms, richly bound with thick coral, adorned with shimmering bracelets and bangles, and joined by armlets and upper-arm ornaments.
Adorned with earrings that brushed against his throbbing arms and ears, [he was like one] upon whose cheeks were reflected the mountain ranges and forested realms of the world. 113.
In whom the moonlight of a gentle smile is enjoyed by the [lips] glowing with passion;
whose eyes are startled by the bees bewildered by the fragrance of her breath;
and who is resplendent with a prominent nose adorned with magnificent pearl ornaments.
The playfulness of her sidelong glances reached the horizons, like the waves of the Yamunā.
In which the bow of Rati’s lover was shaken by the movement of her eyebrows, and which shone with a false musk tilaka as lovely as the half-moon. 116.
Her dark-blue braid rests upon her lotus-like feet, which are adorned with the tips of blue lotuses;
her face, equal to the orb of the moon, is a flowing essence of loveliness.
Sundara beheld Tilottamā, whose beauty surpassed even the splendor of the pollen of his lotus feet; at that moment, his mind was instantly filled with agitation. 118.
Then, like Vairādīva, the merchant Sundara, whose weapon was the flower, pierced the reflection of the city fortress with his arrows during the night.
Oh, what marvelous skill in creation! Oh, what a blossoming of compassion!
Oh, how incomparable is the skill of the Creator in fashioning this armor of beauty! 120.
In their limbs, from the feet to the hair, the two lovely and affectionate lovers have their eyes so deeply immersed in me that they are unable to raise them again. 121.
Is this [reflection] the original of that [face], or is that the original of this? Are these two [breasts] before my eyes a dream or a magical illusion?
These two are full, firm, rounded, and possess a stainless luster.
These two, joined together and moving in unison, possess the characteristic of mutual rivalry. || 123 ||
Beholding the breasts of these two, who could maintain their composure out of indignation?
A single embrace is the fruit of ascetic practices performed over ten million lifetimes.
As for me, what is this [other] nectar of their lips that I have tasted?
I myself pray that I may become the servant of this [Lord], who is the Great Being.
Sundarasvadu said: "I wish to seize Manu with passion.
Attracted by that, he was unable [to do so] and approached the vicinity of these two. 126.
And as they beheld that form of Madana, with its long-lashed eyes,
they became helpless through the onset of the passion of love;
at that very moment, the Mind-born God struck them both simultaneously with his five arrows.
The powerful one, possessing entirely marvelous prowess, pierced through all three.
Pierced by the side-glances of Sundarī’s wife, which were like the playful movements of bees, he sank deep within and fell into a swoon. 129.
And at that very moment,
their hearts, as if pierced by the edge of his sidelong glances, were filled with intense longing. From the mere sight of one another, both of them and that unlovely man [were transformed].
Abandoning their innate fortitude, they were overcome by trembling throughout their limbs.
The suffering bodies of those who had suddenly forgotten their duties and were sighing repeatedly proclaimed the affliction caused by the God of Love. (132)
Then Gaurī, standing nearby,
remembered her husband, the enemy of Smara, just as he had previously been by the side of the Blessed One.
Seeing Sundara’s body withering away throughout his entire life, Hara—
With his face beaming with joy, he spoke while Nanda and the others were listening. ||134||

"Maheśvara, having attained my feet—which are unattainable even for sages who are free from desire and anger and whose vital energy is drawn upward—what has been done by you that is so difficult to achieve? (135)
O handsome one, where liberation is held in the palm of the hand at Kailāsa,
there every desire conceived by the mind is undoubtedly to be enjoyed.
Therefore, having obtained birth on earth, you shall be endowed with those two [qualities] there.
O Bhutkshava, one who knows the Self should enjoy worldly pleasures like a man [who has already tasted them]. || 137 ||
Just as Agastya [spoke], so did the beautiful Īśāna speak to the deer on earth;
and in the same manner, Girijā spoke to them and to her attendants as she had instructed. 138.
Then Sundara, having heard the Śiva-Śambhava curse that was released like a thunderbolt,
prostrated before Īśambhu and spoke thus:
"O God of gods, O Ocean of compassion, O bestower of fearlessness upon devotees!"
O Supreme Lord, forgive this offense and be gracious.
If my birth had occurred on this earth defiled by the Kali age, I would surely forget you;
I would have no memory, like a beast. 141.
Even for great sins born of one's own body, the established rule is that the immediate recollection of Your name is the expiation. O Moon-crested Lord, do not act thus;
show me Your compassion today. (143)
Having bowed hundreds of times with devotion, he wept and clung to the lotus-feet of the Lord.
(End of the fourth chapter of the Sundara-carita in the Bhakta-māhātmya of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. 144.
Then the blessed Lord Hara, the destroyer of obstacles, being pleased,
raised up the beautiful one and spoke with compassion that cooled his limbs. (145)
Maheśvara said: "Listen, O handsome one, to my words; do not weep, for there is no cause for fear.

Even as my own speech never changes, so too shall it be with you. An action performed through lack of discernment may result in great consequences at its fruition. (146) (P.5a, F.6b, 1st line) An action performed through lack of discernment may result in great consequences at its fruition.
Just as poison mixed with food, having entered the stomach through ignorance... (147)

Even Brahmā and the other gods are deluded when defiled by desire and mental constructs (*saṅkalpa*). A living being is bound by mental constructs and is liberated through the absence of mental constructs.
(148) Therefore, people who have me as their sole refuge should abandon all mental constructs.
All are indeed slaves to their own volitions; there is no one who is the master of volition. 149.
Having abandoned me and my own people who partake in my grace, there is my great cosmic illusion (*viśvamāyā*), which is single-minded and consists of gold. 150.
Those who take refuge in me alone are liberated from that illusion.
Through association with women and those attached to women, one becomes possessed by desire. By means of devotion to me, the virtuous person whose intentions are auspicious is liberated.
O Sundara, this has now been seen by you directly with your own eyes. 152.
Since he abandoned my presence and went into the company of women, he has become unworthy of honor; therefore, let there be a fall from his status. 153.
In this very way, Viṣṇu, having descended to earth again and again through his own resolve in the past, subsequently conquered that very resolve. 154.
There shall be no loss of memory for you while yet unborn upon the earth;
let there be full devotion toward me, and let me indeed be present in sacred places.
When the wedding ceremony proceeds there, I, having arrived, [shall behold] the beautiful [scene].
Having fashioned you myself, I shall indeed cut you; of this there is no doubt. (156)
"O handsome one, I have reflected upon this matter; I shall act accordingly for your sake.
O Ramā, you were born near Puṇya, and I have praised you with devotion. (157)
"Having attained supreme fame through his virtuous conduct, he will adorn the earth. Having said this, the Blessed One entered the inner apartments. 158.
Even though he was handsome, Maheśvara, afflicted by despair, prostrated himself and fell from Kailāsa to the earth like the destruction of all the worlds. 159.
The life story of that noble-souled Agastya, beginning with his birth, is [contained] in the Sundara[-kāṇḍa],
which is adorned with a canopy of Śatrughna’s banner and embellished with golden pillars.
Accompanied by his peers, who were adorned with all kinds of ornaments, he went to the bridegroom.
They were adorned with a thousand devoted wives scattering nets of flowers, and with maidens singing. 186.
With rows of lamps like moonlight, its quarters facing all directions, it possessed various kinds of great musical instruments and many meritorious celestial pavilions. 160.
Adorned by Jayabhadra, who possessed the splendor of Śakra, it was perfumed on all sides with incense, like heaven itself. 161.
That assembly hall shone there like the Sudharma hall descended to earth;
and in the midst of the hall stood Sundara, adorned with excellent garments and ornaments. 162.
He trembled as he was carried away by his two brides, like Hari by Śrī and Bhūmi;
there is no one equal to Sundara in the excellence of learning, youth, beauty, wealth, and lineage.
"May there be long life for this noble man together with these two brides upon the earth," the twice-born Indras said.
[Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Bhaktamāhātmya of the Śrī Skanda Purāṇa.]
The assembly hall was adorned with Agastya’s golden vessel, water-jars, parched grain, flowers, sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, sprouts of *dūrvā*, and earthen bowls. (165)
Then, having performed the rite of sowing the sprouts and having tied the auspicious marriage-thread,
the family priest, together with the great men, caused Guṇādhīśa to worship [the deities] and commenced the auspicious wedding ceremony of Sundarī, with her parents' consent having been declared.
Then, within the beautiful interior of the assembly hall, as the resolution for the proposed marriage was being made. (167)
There was seen a certain very old man, a leader of people,
leaning upon a bamboo staff, stumbling at every step,
with the hair between his eyebrows and on his eyelashes white with grey.
Adorned with earrings, tall in stature, and his hair bound with a white turban. ||199||
His limbs were smeared with ashes and adorned with rudrākṣa beads and blood; he wore saffron-colored garments and had two teeth like the throat of a goat. 200.
Beholding him in the midst of the assembly—his beauty enhanced by the rays of his teeth, and marked with the emblem of the throat of Śiva—the assembled brahmins rose up;
some, having offered the *arghya* water, bowed at his feet. (201)
Others, however, out of devotion, offered him a hand to hold; others gave [it] with great respect. (202) And the Treasure of the Vedas also offered a great seat before him.
The children laughed with clapping hands and were full of mischief.
But Sundī, beholding him wearing ashes and rudrākṣa beads, thought in her mind:
"He is either some devotee resembling Śailādī, or perhaps Śiva himself;
in any case, he is certainly worthy of worship. (204)
Then, once that old man was seated, Śivavrata said this to him: || 205 ||
"You are a great Brahmin; from where have you come? What indeed is your name?
By the sight of you, we have achieved our purpose; here is our hospitality for you. (206)
"O observer of the Śiva-vow, my residence is always in the city of Kamalā.
I know you, but do you ever know us?
Let this discussion rest for now; what is this assembly here, and what is the ritual? (207)
What has become of the sound of the musical instruments here— has it been reduced to nothing by the cries of children?
(208, 6th line) A handsome man named Kamalālayanātha, who observes the vow of Śiva, was made [to perform] sacrifices.

"O son, having attained mastery over all branches of knowledge through your arduous penance, this marriage has been proposed for you; may it be fulfilled by your blessings. Having spoken thus, while he was still restraining Śiva from his vow, the most excellent of elders [spoke].
The assembly spoke with faltering words:
"Something is being said in our hearts that we, the great people, do not understand. (211)
"Speak all of you with restraint; let it be the truth alone, not a falsehood.

This beautiful man, a devotee of Śiva, has been purchased by me as a slave through labor. Having caused him to forget his past, that fool-souled man has forcibly adopted him here as a son. (212) (9th line) Having caused him to forget [his origin], that deluded soul has taken him as a son here by force.
Having counted [the days] after my departure, he even caused my marriage to be performed. || 213 ||
"What effort can be made for one who is merely a bone in the form of a son? This is truly said:
even Kubera is equal to Śrīdāman; what then of others? (2.14)
I shall cause this servant to perform every duty that is required of him whenever the desire arises within me.
There are millions of my servants who dwell at the ends of the quarters.
Just as prosperity has been bestowed upon him as was fitting, let this [other] also be likewise.
"O beautiful slave, why have you entered his house leaving me behind? Arise, let us go; I shall give you whatever you desire. 217.
When Agastya spoke thus, that assembly became bewildered;
wonder arose in the minds of the bride, the groom, and their kinsmen. (218)
At the edge of the tumultuous crowd, the learned men, experts in legal procedure and renowned in all directions, were urged by Jayabhadra. (219) The Brāhmaṇas said:
"You are old, yet you prattle as if you were capable in worldly affairs;
this meaning of the scriptures is nowhere to be found—that a twice-born man may perform a purchased rite."

Whether it be due to the fatigue of the journey or prompted by old age, this speech has been endured; therefore, O Great King Jayabhadra, remain patient and silent, for supreme patience is beautiful. (221)
The teacher, who does not become angry at wicked speech regarding any branch of knowledge,
is aged; neither desire nor anger exists in me toward my servants.
For this alone is renowned as the sole defining characteristic of our servitude.
O observer of the Śiva-vow, why do you speak such confused words? In that case, I can no longer tolerate it.
Having banished him, let the undertaking of the work proceed once it has been fixed outside.
"O elder, is this land without a king? Are there no virtuous men in the city?
For I, a slave to one whose movement is unbound by serpents, am being led away by others. (225)
"Speak the truth, O Sundara; practice righteousness, O blameless one! You are my servant; speak something here in the presence of all. 226. Sundara said:
The Brahmin spoke words that were inconsistent with his meditative cultivation, as if he were still bound by worldly truth:
"We are the servants of Śambhu, we who dwell in the abode of Kamalā.
The servant of Hara is not the servant of another; for him, the entire world serves as a servant. (227)
He who offers a servant to Hara as a servant employed for Śiva shall become a bearer [of his burden]. || 228 ||
If Śaṅkara does not tolerate you entering his house while you bear ashes and rudrākṣas, then I bow to you; let this speech be withdrawn. 229.
"O Vṛddha, what is it that you say, O Sundara? What is lacking for you in my presence? O Sundara, I look upon you no differently than upon my two sons. (230) (4th line)
"Sundara, I do not know you; there has been no association with you in this birth.
Even if great men were to speak a falsehood, who could prevent it? (231)
O elders, listen to me: there is a document in my hand witnessed [by others]. I am committing this act of violence against one who has written it with his own hand. 232.

"O Brahmins, show the document! This writing was made by Vṛddhayu; it is established for both parties. If the testimony of women is not authoritative, then let her two [male] relatives be the witnesses on the document."
Come there and ask them; look for the letter right there.
"Agastya," said the Blessed Śambhu, appearing in the guise of an old man;
"you have wandered for a long time"—saying this, he suddenly appeared before Sundara. (234)
The elder, having gone out ahead, went back behind as he questioned [him];
though the elder followed Sundara, he did not go even two steps. Having traversed the path, Kamalā [remained] within the city.
He entered the inner palace, which was adorned with jeweled gate-towers.
"Who is the witness here? O elder, show him this document! Having thus called out, Sundara fearlessly went to the door of the monastery. (239)
He stood for a moment in wonder, desiring the departure of the elder;
then [Śiva] appeared together with Umā, endowed with all excellent qualities,
mounted upon a divine bull and accompanied by Skanda and Vighneśvara.
Having reached the gateway, he was being praised by the foremost of the gods.
Beholding Sundara standing there, his lotus-like face smiling, he showed him to the Mountain, declaring, "This Sundara is my servant. (242)
With a sidelong glance at the maiden, he spoke again to Sundara.
[Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Vibhāva," in the *Sundara-carita* within the *Śivabhakta-māhātmya* of the glorious *Skanda Purāṇa*. (243) (4th line)
Maheśvara said:
"O Sundara, as for what was spoken by you in the presence of many—that 'I am not your servant'—let this be proven; why do you delay? (244)
This Gaurī, the mother of the worlds, is the witness to your service;
likewise, these two—the elephant-faced one and the six-faced one—are also here upon the earth. 245.
Sundara beheld the Lord of the Gaṇas, accompanied by Umā and Skanda, mounted upon a bull,
holding a large letter in his right hand,
with his lotus feet being praised by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas. ||246||
The leader of the host, having sounded the drums and trumpets, offered his praise.
With a bewildered heart, having closed his eyes for a moment and then opening them again toward Sundara, he bowed down to him. 248.

The Blessed One, who is at the forefront of all worlds, having himself summoned with respect that creator—Brahmā—who delights in a false self, speaks false words, and finds pleasure in falsehood, along with Hari, Rudra, and the others;
who is unknown even by the mind and is eternal... to that great God, beloved of his devotees, to You, [I offer] salutation. 250.
Sometimes he is inauspicious, sometimes auspicious, and never joined with name or form;
homage to him, homage to him—homage to that Great One!
Salutations to that Great God, by whose glance this illusion became the means of creation;
salutations to that Great God. (252) Salutations to that Great God, whose power is Māyā, which is the limit of greatness and sovereignty; salutations to that Great God. (254)

Salutations, salutations to Him by whose power the threefold ego (ahaṅkāra) was born from the Great One (mahat), and from whom, when impelled, the creation of the elements, the senses, and the mind arose. Salutations, salutations. 257.
Salutations, salutations to Him by whom the five elements were placed [in order], and even those [elements] which have no mutual connection. Salutations, salutations.
Salutations, salutations to him who, having entered those [beings], is divided according to the forms of Virāṭ;
salutations, salutations to him who, joined with speech through the desire to create, creates the entire universe to be created;
salutations, salutations to Hari, who, adorned by Śrī, extends protection for that [universe]. 259.
Salutations to him, salutations to him, whose form is the left side of the Daughter of the Mountain, who brings about the destruction of that which is otherwise difficult to achieve. 260.
Salutations again and again to Him who stands as the witness of the Prājña, Taijasa, and Viśva states, and as the enjoyer of that which is to be enjoyed;
salutations again and again to Him who remains having pervaded everything in the form of food (annam). 261.
Salutations again and again to Him in whom this universe is woven like a string of gems upon a thread,
who abides within as the conscious Self, yet is not perceived by the senses; salutations again and again to Him,
attached to whom the world is attached, and by whom everything vibrates.
Salutations, salutations to Him, wherein the various manifestations of conceptual proliferation appear like whirlpools in the ocean. 263.
Salutations, salutations to that self-luminous Lord who is of one and the same form in the beginning, at the end, and in the middle; he who is the golden Person shining within the solar orb. 264.

Even the gods were struck with wonder; how much more so, then, was Śambhu, let alone a mortal on earth? ||341||
We bow at his feet; those people there have brought forth a beautiful Hara, having realized the Saṅkalpa-Bhairava of the God of inconceivable power.
"O beautiful one who has entered into the darkness of my ego!
How can such great grace from the Lord be directed toward me?"—thinking thus, O Śambhu, he redoubled his devotion. (343)
Having bowed to Naṭeśa in the assembly hall, and having saluted the sages beginning with Vyāsa, as well as Nandin and the other lords of the Gaṇas, and the great devotees of Śiva; ||344||
Having obtained the permission of Gaurī and the Lord, the Master of the Assembly of Consciousness, the glorious Sundara, the protector of Śiva’s command, departed. 345.
Having turned back all his followers and paid homage to the one of foremost birth (Brahmā),
he crossed the Uttarakāverī and proceeded toward Brahmapura,
where the child Bodhasambandhaka resides as an incarnation of Skanda.
From tasting the nectar of Gaurī’s breast-milk, she caused Bhāratī to dance.
This very path, purified by the dust of the lotus feet of the one connected to awakening, is not fit to be touched by this assembly; thus [the Lord] is truly beautiful. (348)
Standing at a distance, he praised those whose bodies were like Kailāsa; then Maheśvara, together with Gaurī, manifested himself and took refuge within him.
The Lord, the master of Kailāsa, bestowed his grace upon him. (349)
Then, having thus taken leave of him, he went toward the southern direction with his head bowed.
Beholding the splendor of the expanse of the illustrious Colaviṣaya, he went to the bank of the Kāverī, adorned by the station of Kapardin. (351)
Having plunged into the holy river Kāverī, which originates from the mountains,
he rejoiced as he gazed all around at that great river,
whose vast pools were filled with the intense fragrance of lotuses, water-lilies, and white lilies. (352) (9th line)
It was like a mass of camphor, with its great expanse of sandy banks appearing as a shimmering circle.
The interior of the plantain groves rivaled the *hintāla* and *kramuka* trees, with juices extracted from coconut fruits worn away by wild asses. (354)

Even in the heat of summer, the milk-rivers, with their waves scattered by the blows from the mountain peaks of the breasts of the wives of merchants— who were wringing out their fine cotton garments— attained a state equal to the waters of the rainy season.
(355) (Second line) [The rivers] bore the moisture squeezed out by the wives of the merchants as they wrung their fine cotton garments.
Adorned with the circles of rut-fluid from the intoxicated elephants of the enemy's army. ||356||

The great heat of the sun was blocked by the shade of the thickets of wild trees; it was filled with the mingled sounds of crickets, peacocks, pigeons, and bees; and it was purified by the sound of the Vedānta from the groups of sages in their huts on the bank. 357.
(3rd line) [It was] purified by the sound of the Vedānta from the multitude of sages in the huts on the bank.
It was adorned with rows of sacrificial posts belonging to great sacrificers who were constant performers of rituals.
Beholding the Kāverī, that great river who is the consort of the Lord of the Great Ocean, whose waves are drenched in yogic sleep,
that great poet visited the shrines of Paśupati.
Māyūra, Madhyārjuna, Kumbhaghoṇa, Śrīvañci, and Japyeśvara—these are the names [of the sacred sites].
Having visited the divine sites and departed from Niṣevya, he went to the city of Satyāgarāja.
[Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Śivabhaktamāhātmya of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. 361.
O twice-born ones, hear now another wonderful deed of Agastya performed for Carita-sundara,
which is renowned throughout all the worlds and destroys all sins.
What is difficult to obtain when the Lord whose banner is the bull is pleased?
Nevertheless, O Hari, out of devotion, devotees desire nothing other than Him;
wherever there is a station of Śiva, there indeed is Sundara.
Praising the God accompanied by Bhavānī with joy, he went to his preceptor.

Then, having attained faith, Sundara—whose speech was beautiful—entered the city of Kamalālaya. There, having been asked for his welfare by the local inhabitants, he bowed before the presence of the King of Generosity (Avalokiteśvara) and desired to offer praise upon seeing him. (365)
The eloquent speech of that Maheśa increased [his] prosperity. ||366||
Before the ocean whose form is the rising moon, the beautiful one stands motionless on the shore;
in another age, he was Viṣṇu, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace. (367)
Having been propitiated by all the gods and the Asuras, Aditi’s sons,
he mounted the lord of birds and advanced to fight the Daityas; there,
a great battle between the gods and the Asuras took place.
No one had his head crushed by the mace. ||369||
They were rendered unconscious by the sound of the Śārṅga bow, cut down by the sharp edge [of the arrow], and swept far away like riverbanks by the flapping of the wings of the Lord of Birds. 370.

The Daityas took refuge in Hari for the sake of crossing over ignorance; having entered the Veda as their sanctuary, they perceived the sage Bhṛgu, who was oppressed by Hari, as the embodiment of the Asuras' fatigue.
(371) (3rd line) Having entered the Veda as their sanctuary, they beheld the sage Bhṛgu.
The Daityas attained the supreme state by reaching the wife of the sage while she was pregnant.
Having been told [this] by Bhṛgu’s wife, who had been granted fearlessness, he entered the interior of a Daitya;
not seeing the sage there, Hari turned back on his path.
From the fire impelled by the gods, he learned of the activities of the enemies of the immortals.
The gods of heaven, having found no refuge, were tormented by the human king.
Having reached the hermitage of Bhārgava, the king of birds descended.
Seeing that Viṣṇu had arrived, the illustrious wife of Bhṛgu [welcomed him]. (375)
With palms joined in reverence, she offered the guest-offering (arghya) and inquired after his welfare;

then that virtuous woman spoke these words with a voice as sweet as that of a monkey, delighted by the sight of him as if she had suddenly found a long-lost treasure. (376) (6th line) She was overjoyed at the sight of him, like one who has recently acquired a hidden hoard.
O Lord of Śrī, O Lord of the Earth, O God, salutations be unto you, O Lord of the World! ||377||
Be gracious toward me, your devotee, O Keśava, who are kind to your devotees!
By your name, Ādi and Ananta, you are the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of all that is visible. (378)
"Your praise is unknown even to Brahmā and the other gods; you have been seen by me through my good fortune, as well as by great sages devoted to austerity, with ancient speech. (379)
The great-souled ones are pleased when honored with leaves, flowers, and fruits; they do not grant favor for any other reason. What is the purpose of your coming? (380)
"O Lord of Umā, favor us with your sweet, nectar-like speech.
Thus honored by his wife, that man who is the eye of Bhṛgu’s lineage,
wearing a forest garland, remained there in wonder.
Viṣṇu said: Listen to my words, O virtuous one; I have been honored by you, O sinless lady. (382)

"Afflicted by fear of the gods and Daityas, they have come to me, the protector, for refuge. Therefore, I have made an effort to destroy those Daityas in order to protect them. While the Daityas are being slain by me, some Dānavas—"
"We have reached your inner chamber," she heard from the mouth of the fire-god.
"Your husband worships the gods; they are well-disposed toward you, O virtuous wife.
Tell me where I may slay the Dānavas with my discus while they are hidden.
(385) Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, she spoke again to her devoted husband.
Having closed the door of the leaf-hut, they were indeed afraid because of this base act. ||386||

O Teacher of the World, though you are the primordial person, Vidura and others do not hold you as dear as they hold the Dharma, which is the source of all activity and the protector of the world. (4th line) Even one who is beloved is not as dear to you as the Dharma. O Teacher of the World, you uphold the Dharma that governs the course of worldly existence.
How is it that by the instigation of Varuṇa you have become an enemy, while the Daityas have come to me for refuge, just as the enemies of the Asuras have come to you?
(388) There is no greater sin than abandoning one who has sought refuge;
in this regard, they cite this ancient history. (386)
Having given his own body’s flesh to the hawk, Śaibya indeed protected the dove that had come for refuge;
thus he attained great fame. One should protect even an enemy who has come for refuge as a dove does;
even when faced with the danger to one's own life, one must not abandon one who has sought protection. (391)
"O Daityas, though born in hell for as long as the moon and stars endure, I shall not abandon Viṣṇu, for he is my refuge. (392)
Then, having first [attacked] Vajrāhi and afterwards the Dānavas who cause destruction, he blocked the door of the house where the devoted wife of the Guru resided. (393)
Urged by the gods, Viṣṇu struck [Hiraṇyakaśipu] with his discus;
having slain the Dānavas, he subsequently protected the inhabitants of heaven.
Enraged because [his son] had restored his wife to life through knowledge and asceticism, Bhṛgu [cursed him]. (394)
Viṣṇu cursed Keśava as well, saying, "You shall suffer the pain of separation from a woman," and having abandoned him who was pursued by the sin of slaughter, he went to the abode of Kamalā.
Having reached the abode of Kamalā, [Keśava remained] for the sake of removing the sin of slaughter from his devotee.

Priyātā worshipped the Blessed Maheśvara. (398) Then Viṣṇu, having gathered the lords of sages and the gods, asked his own laughter for a means of atonement, even though he had already attained the glory of his desires. (399) (*3rd line*)
Having propitiated Keśava, who is supported by sages and gods, the sages [should act] so that he may be released through the performance of expiatory rites. ||400||
The one of great wisdom did not reproach him; he became one whose anger was stilled.
With his wrath appeased, the great sage spoke these words to Śriya’s beloved: 401.
"O Madhusūdana, even in hundreds of Viṣṇu-kalpas, the sin of killing an embryo cannot be averted by you;
yet, O Slayer of Madhu, if you were not angry with me, there would have been peace.
Because I was entreated by the gods and the twice-born, forgiveness arose in me through my vision. (402)
The virtuous do not retaliate even against those who have committed offenses, even if they are like you.
Nevertheless, the Noble One will show favor to those who are stricken with grief; yet there is no atonement for this transgression—nevertheless, let this be heard. (404)
By reciting the great mantra of the Rudrādhyāya twelve crores of times,
and by performing an ablution with milk upon the Śiva-liṅga, expiation is achieved.
Furthermore, lying upon a bed of ashes and likewise covered in ashes, perform [the rite].
"Furthermore, by serving Soma and Skanda, you shall attain even greater prosperity.
Having spoken thus, the great sage returned to his own hermitage with his disciples;
Hari, however, continued for a long time to repeat the mantra of the Śatarudrīya.
While the wish-fulfilling [cow] was consecrating Maheśvara with streams of milk upon the divine linga of marble for many divine groups of years,
at the dissolution of ten koṭis of padmas, an incorporeal voice arose.
The sin of foeticide has dissolved away from you; O Prajāviśvambhara, may you possess prosperity.
"You are weary from your progeny today; what more do you desire?
O Viṣṇu, listen to such words as these with joined palms. (410)
He replied, "O Lord, if the slaughter has been destroyed by your worship, O moon-crested one, I desire to behold your true form directly.
O God Śaṅkara, you who are affectionate toward your devotees, grant me this boon. (411)
"Even a doer of evil, by meditating upon it, may assume whatever form you possess. (412)
One is immediately liberated from all sins born of speech, mind, and body.
Thus Hari spoke to Vāśva, who was making this request. 413.
Even Brahmā and the hosts of gods, as well as Agastya and other yogis,
though they have performed hundreds of sacrifices, given abundant gifts,
and even worshipped me in the form of a *liṅga*, remain with their hearts stolen by craving.
They are unable to see me without the cessation of the mind.
Listen, O Viṣṇu, to these words if you desire to see me for two crores of years together with the splendor of one who has conquered the senses. (5th line) 416.
"Being detached from all enjoyments, practice the Pāśupata vow;
then, when the appointed time is complete on my account, I shall show myself to you.
You shall behold that form of mine which is seen by yogins. (417)
Having thus spoken on the mountain peak as the waters subside like waves,
the Lord Janārdana undertook initiation into the Pāśupata vow;
having smeared himself with ashes and bound his hair in a topknot, he wore garments of bark and bore matted locks.
Devoted to the worship at the six times of the day and night, he remained for twenty days standing in water up to his neck, reciting the five-syllabled mantra of Japan. ||420||
Having obtained her husband once more by the command of Śiva, Kamalā also undertook an excellent vow dedicated to the Great God;
and having learned that he was liberated from the sin of slaughter, she became his attendant there.
With beautiful and variegated lotus-stalk ornaments, she worshipped Maheśvara. ||422||
It is fitting that Kamalā sports with those very blossoming *jevvantikā* flowers in the place named Kamalālaya, while Madhusūdana sports with them as well. 423.
The devoted one worshipped with the *Śivasahasranāma*,
surpassing [all others] with an offering of camphor paste and a garland of *kahlāra* buds. When two years had passed, Candraśekhara was highly pleased.
Having assumed the body of Somāskanda, Hara bestowed grace upon Viṣṇu.
[He was seen] together with the daughter of the mountain king and the six-faced one, [having been worshipped] by the slayer of Madhu from the Liṅga of the lowest essence.
Śambhu (Śiva) shall appear before him, his beautiful cheeks smeared with camphor paste and his body fragrant with the blood of the Saugandhika lotus.
[Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Śivabhaktamāhātmya of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. (427) Sundara beheld Mahādeva, who had manifested as Somāskanda, standing before him.
The quarters of the sky were perfumed by the application of camphor and the scent of white lotuses;
he bore matted locks that possessed the brilliant luster of molten gold.
The slender crescent moon upon her head, white as a lotus stalk. 429.
Indeed, Gaṅgā, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva likewise [are his forms];
he bears a beautiful deer-essence mark upon his crest. 430.
Resplendent with ear-ornaments of blooming *javanikā* flowers.
He has a radiant forehead-mark born of Kāśmīra, eyes like blazing fire,
beautiful creeper-like eyebrows, and a gaze with side-long glances of intense compassion.
Her lotus-face, with its bimba-fruit-like cheeks reflected in her mirror-like temples, possesses a row of teeth possessing the luster of pearls strung together.
Her sprout-like lower lip, soft and possessing the luster of coral,
was graced by the beauty of a chin that was round like a moon and shone from her face.
The smearing of the throat with the luster of *kālakūṭa* and *prabhāmīśraka*,
along with jeweled rings, bracelets, armlets, bangles, and upper-arm ornaments.
His hands brandish the axe, the deer, the gesture of granting boons (*vara-mudrā*), and the thunderbolt;
he possesses a fragrant garland of *saugandhika* lotuses from which bees are driven away by its scent.
He is the abode for the mountain maidens, the earth, the waters, and the creepers, who do not turn their faces away from his limbs. 436.
His navel is filled with the luster of the ruby from the *nāga* at Oḍyāṇa;
his abdomen is adorned with the brilliance of the gold-plate of her necklace of star-like pearls; he wears a sacred thread [in the form of] the ash-smear produced by his exhalation.
437. (2nd line) His sacred thread is indeed the ash-smear produced by his breath.
Clad in a tiger skin and adorned with jeweled anklets.
Indeed, with its upraised hood, it possesses sandals reddened by the luster of the crest-jewel on its head;
it is like the sun that dispels the darkness of the meditator’s ego-conceit, shining from the palm of its hand. 439.
Resplendent with the brilliance of nails like water-lilies upon the chest of Kāla, it was like a fresh sprout on the tree that brings about the kalpa of absolute liberation (kaivalya). 440.
It bestows devotion and fearlessness, adorned with tinkling bells; it is the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra, possessing the majesty of its own supreme splendor. 441.
Bearing a beautiful lotus that resembles the petals of a blooming water-lily, he is seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, his form most exceedingly lovely. (442)

The goddess, daughter of the King of Mountains, adorned with every ornament, appeared like the beauty of the jewel of life unfolding, surrounded by a halo, as if dwelling upon his left side—she whose eyes were as long as the *pārijāta* flower. 443.
(6th line) The goddess, daughter of the King of Mountains, adorned with every ornament.
And [he saw] the prince of delicate form playing between those two. ||444||
He was adorned with anklets, tinkling bells, a girdle, armlets, bracelets, and upper-arm ornaments, as well as with costly garlands and finger-rings. 445.
Resplendent with an ear-ornament embraced by a tiger’s claw,
with six rising trunks of elephants and twelve shimmering earrings,
[the face] was rendered enchanting by gentle smiles flowing from its corners.
She was perfected by means of eyes whose pupils were tremulous with side-long glances adored by people. ||447||
With lips like coral adorned by droplets of Ambikā’s breast-milk, and with playful curls of hair and forehead marks of musk; 448.

With dark, curly locks embraced by crest-jewels, with the regions of their foreheads pierced by the light of dangling gems, and with six lotus-faces whose smiles were fragrant with the scent of their sighs; 449. (P.21b, F.118a, 1st line) [They appeared] with teeth that seemed to be gazing out.
Beholding him, he was overwhelmed with joy and fell at his feet. ||450||
Having prostrated and praised him ten million times, with palms joined in reverence along with Śrī, she held above him a parasol fashioned from peacock feathers. (451)
Filled with overflowing joy, Śivāṇī, victorious over all, meditated upon the excellent sound of the Pāñcajanya conch from the Cañcāmaragaccha. 452.
Beholding the Lord before him, Hari attained such bliss that even the bliss of Brahman could not equal even a fraction of it. (453)
Then the Lord of Gods, Maheśvara, accompanied by Umā and Skanda, being pleased, spoke with a smile to Janārdana, who stood before him with palms joined in reverence:
"The sin of foeticide has been removed from you; you have once again been united with Śrī."
"By this practice of vows, she has now attained equality with me.
Let her sovereignty over the three worlds remain as it was before—unobserved by others and invisible even to yogins. (455–456)
Those highly fortunate ones who serve him as he sits upon the jeweled lion-throne together with Skanda and his consort are established in that which brings about liberation. 457.
"You are exhausted from wandering for a very long time, O Viṣṇu; what else do you desire?
Viṣṇu said:
"O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord, may you always remain in this form out of grace toward me. (458) (7th line)
May the gods and sages be satisfied by the sight of you;
O Lord, grant us your permission for the practice of yogic sleep. 459.
Thus requested by him, Śambhu assumed that very form;
and upon seeing him in such a state, the gods became pure of heart toward the yogin.
Whatever was most dear to each person, by giving that away to others,
he attained the title "Lord of Renunciation" (Tyāgeśvara), which is beyond the reach of mind and speech.
Then, after some time had passed, a man who dwelt in the great ocean [appeared].
Having placed the Lord Attyāgeśvara within a casket of jewels for me.
Having placed [the child] upon his chest and having received permission from Maheśvara, he fell asleep;
for the Lord of Kamalā was overcome by sleep due to the force of his own inhalations and exhalations. (463)
Then, having beheld the dance of the swan-like Lord of Girijā, the yogis praised the God who was intensely engaged in the *tāṇḍava* dance. 464.
They abandoned the suffering of saṃsāra upon reaching the chest of Kāśyapa.
Then, when Indra, fearing the asuras,
made his request, Hari rose up, gave his own chest to Indra, and went to Hara.
Day after day, victory shall be yours over him. ||466||
Having instructed him thus and having slain the Dānavas with his discus, Viṣṇu, the Lord Hari, established [the world] and lay down upon his couch in the ocean. 467.
Indra, too, by performing daily the ritual of worship for the King of Trees (the *aśvattha*) together with Śacī,
attained great prosperity.
(468) With the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā, a large parasol, the sounds of conchs, and sacred mantras—
Having worshipped Śambhu with offerings of blood, Javvantikā attained the splendor of Hari, just as Mukunda did.
(6th line) [Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Śivabhaktamāhātmya of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. 470.
In the meantime, the Lord Maheśvara, together with the Goddess, arrived at the grove of Mount Kailāsa, where the trees were in full bloom;
it was as if strewn with camphor dust exhaled by royal plantain trees. ||471||
It was white with the pollen of golden lotuses as if with saffron;
it was reddish where there were young dūrvā grasses, and dark in some places due to intoxicated bees.
It was graced by birds of many colors warbling their songs, [as he observed] his vow.
Having entered the grove like a lover approaching a passionate woman, Hari—who removes the pride of Kāma—adorned it with fresh flowers. (474)
She wore a *karṇikāra* flower in her hair, a lotus-stamen ornament on her ears,
a beautiful *puṇṇāga* bud upon the tip of her prominent nose,
lodhra pollen on her cheeks, and a charming *karṇikā* on her forehead. (475)
A garland made of sinduvāra flowers and bracelets of lotus stalks.
Gaurī, whose breasts were adorned with lines of hair and who bore a flower-ornament upon her hand, delighted Hara with her great fruitfulness. 477.
At the foot of a *śrīphala* tree, Hara, whose abode is the cave of all things, seated Śivā upon his lap on a bed of flowers; at that time,
the sun hung over the edge of the western mountain.
By good fortune, at that time, even the night of evil omens became purifying for the sinners as well. ||479||
At that time, a certain man named Romaśa, whose face was as white as a *gula* fruit, worshipped Śambhu with *vilva* leaves there and was liberated. (480)
Bending his branch with a subtle curve, he alighted upon the tip of a *śrīphala* tree;
having rested there, by the power of his innate supernatural success, he caused that branch to move.
He then broke off tender and uninjured *bilva* leaves.
All those leaves fall upon the surface of the earth. ||482||
By good fortune, they fell at the feet of the Lord who was united with Gaurī;
the Lord counted them until they reached one hundred and eight. 483.
Showing himself to Gaurī, he looked at her with a sidelong glance;
then the Lord, the Master of Beasts, rose up and was embraced by her. (484)
He called out, "Come! to the monkey who was atop the bilva tree;
at that moment, having gained consciousness, he leaped from the top of that tree.
Having circumambulated him, he fell at the feet of Śiva and Pārvatī.
The Blessed Lord Īśvara, pleased by his worship with bilva leaves, spoke to him: 486.
Having been a sovereign ruler for one hundred thousand and eight years, and having become a lord of the mandala, you shall at the end attain my own state.
Go to the earth; O sinless one, let your birth be within the lineage of Manu.
Thus addressed, Pūridant replied to Maheśvara:
"O Lord, grant this Lāṅgūla the sovereignty; that is not what I desire.
Even if I were to perform service at your feet, should I be born [again]? (488–489)
O Supreme Lord, be gracious! When shall my livelihood be secured?
May there be eternal devotion for me at your lotus feet. (490) You ought not to grant me a kingdom that is an obstacle to service at your feet.
I become a slave here; I do not go to take birth upon this earth.

Where one of unclouded intellect, having understood [the truth], does not perceive through learning, age, or views, nor through noble lineage, he attains the ultimate end. (492) [He attains it] when endowed with the fourfold army, possessing all enjoyments and prosperity.
"I give you the kingdom"—such was the deception practiced by Citra toward Nala.
If you are pleased, O Compassionate One, let my lion-throne be yours;
nothing else is desired by me, nor do I serve you for the sake of prosperity. (494) Where there is no service to you both, there birth is without darkness.
Be gracious, O ocean of compassion; may your mercy be upon me. ||495||
To him who was thus grieving, the Bull-bannered Lord spoke words of consolation:
"Listen; do not give way to despondency, but act according to what has been commanded. (496)

Worship performed out of ignorance leads to worldly enjoyment, whereas worship preceded by realized knowledge leads to liberation; this has been established in thousands of Vedas and Agamas by those most learned in the Vedas. (Verse 497, line 6) The fruit obtained from worshipping with even a single bilva leaf at dusk is immeasurable.
I shall proclaim that secret; listen, for you shall partake in its fruit.
One who is dispassionate and recognizes my transgression, having worshipped me, is liberated.
Through ignorance or by chance, she bestows upon me the enjoyment of my subjects and the kingdom. (499)
Then, having attained your own [true] nature and experiencing for one birth the enjoyments desired by the gods,
you will certainly reach my feet at the end of that life through my grace.
There, upon seeing the two horses, a friendship with Hari will arise within you.
"You are my devotee; you ought not to feel distress, O Bhūcchāma. ||501||
Thus addressed, he spoke again to his ministers regarding this matter;
there, though exceedingly emaciated, he said "So be it" and vanished.
(502) Born with the face of a golangula monkey, he was born into the lineage of Manu.
I bow to that [Goddess] who is capable of enduring the king and others, just as a husband [endures his wife]. ||503||
Once, for the sake of victory over the Daityas, the friend of the mute Ajagṛṅga was summoned by his companion, who was himself a master of the Vajra. (504)
Having conquered the Dānavas along with Indra, the king entered heaven;
welcomed by all the gods and receiving blessings from his preceptor,
he sat down upon an excellent throne together with Mahendra.
He had taken half the seat of the victorious Arjuna, possessing the form of one whose eyes were fixed on the god of love;
his chest was adorned with the color of the tips of the arrows from the army of the enemies of the gods,
and he was beautified by nail-marks as if by a choice lover for the sake of the Goddess of Victory.
There, the celestial damsels waited upon the king:
Rambhā held the fly-whisk, and Menakā likewise held the water-pitcher;
Sukeśī held the palm-leaf fan, and Mañjughoṣā held the betel-roll.
May Tilottamā bestow upon him the excellence of dancing and the glory of her head.
Vīṇāvatī, Citralekhā, Sahajanyā holding the rhythmic beat,
and the Gandharvas accompanied by song, waited upon Mucukunda with great devotion.
Then, after the music had been praised, when the sun had reached the middle of the sky, Indra, having mounted the neck of Airāvata, went to his inner apartments. (511)
Indrāṇī maintained her conduct like Mucukunda and Mukunda;
having bathed in the waters of the Mandākinī, both the lord of men and Mahendra went to the abode of the subjects of Purāri,
which was adorned with jewels.

There, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrabhṛt), adorned with ashes and rudrākṣa beads, began the worship of the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva) with incense of divine agallochum. Mucukunda, the royal sage whose prowess was equal to that of Mukunda (Viṣṇu), also [began his worship]. ||513-514||
Having seen Mahādeva Somāskanda, his hair stood on end with joy; [hearing] his very words, he praised Śiva mentally with ashes and parched grain. 515.
Satisfied by this secret hymn of praise, the Lord Īśvara, the Master of Creatures, whispered into his ear: "O King, conquer the Brāhmaṇas. (516)
Agitated by that service, O protector of the earth, the Lord of Śacī did not perceive him as he was about to depart for the surface of the world at the end of the creation. 517.
"What do you desire? he asked, while embracing him firmly.
Then, taking Indra by the hand, the lord of the earth said this:
"If you have any affection for me, give him to me along with Soma and Skanda."
Having formed this resolve, I desire to procreate offspring out of my affection for you.
O protector of the earth, Indra also spoke privately with a smiling face:
"Friend, I tell you this truth; why should it be hidden from you by me? (520)
Know this to be the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Viṣṇu; it is enjoined for his worship alone.
O King, this same [practice] exists among your subjects as well.
(4th line) If Hari is pleased with you, pray to this Lord of Śrī.
Then [he thought], "I shall be the giver of this gift; he is the master of it, even otherwise. ||522||
Having heard these words of Indra, he meditated upon Maheśvara in his heart.
Commanded by Him, "Go," he went swiftly and was released at Vaikuṇṭha. (523)
Having bowed and praised him in many ways, he entreated Keśava;
and Keśava, having meditated for a moment at the command of the Supreme Lord, granted his permission. Then, returning once more to the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra), he [reported].
"O Jiṣṇu, you have received permission from Viṣṇu; O Maheśvara, grant it [to me]!
The appointed time is passing away, and I shall cause the earth to be measured [by my stride] out of friendship.
Having heard the king’s words, he fell into deep thought: "How indeed [shall this be]? (525-526)
"Let him take this; I shall give it away. These days will pass away empty [of me].
How indeed could King Mucukunda remain when his desires are fulfilled? (527)

Having observed that the wise man, through his proximity, has transcended the creator (Tvaṣṭṛ), he would not perceive the support [of the reflection], for it is merely imagined as a reflection of this [creator]. (528)
Having fashioned the images, even Viśvakarman gave them to the Lord of Śacī;
having delivered the crafted image, he addressed him, saying, "Depart. (529)
Taking up [the image] again and again, the king said to his friend:
"Grant me an unimagined boon; do not deceive me.
Hari gave him six images that had been fashioned again and again.
Having accepted those, he then desired to perform the seventh [rite] once more.
O enemy of Vṛtra, if the embodied soul were to directly impel the Lord—the unconditioned Maheśāna—then there would be strife. ||532||
Then, having conciliated King Somāskanda,
the Lord of Śacī presented him to the king as Maheśvara mounted upon a jeweled lion-throne;
he also gave him a great parasol, a conch shell, and the *jaupanti* flower.
Always wear a garland of white water-lilies and apply camphor ointment. (534)
Having thus addressed the protector of the earth, he sent him toward the cow;
and Mucukunda, his mind filled with joy, circumambulated the earth. (535)
On the highest peak of the mountain, within the lotus-dwelling body of the earth,
he was commanded to protect the world and installed Maheśa;
having established the supreme *kalās* in the six locations all around.
Constantly worshipping Kīrti, he attained eternal and stainless purity. Then the Lord, being pleased, first favored Viṣṇu, then Mahendra immediately thereafter, and finally Mucukunda. ||537-538||

Salutations to Śiva, who is smeared with camphor, who possesses all arts, whose neck is adorned with garlands of white water-lilies, who is like the wish-fulfilling tree for those who take refuge in his lotus feet, and who bestows liberation. 539.

Thus, delighted by the nectar of Sundara’s beautiful verses, may the Blessed One—who is adorned with the crescent of the young moon and whose crown shines with its imagined luster—be compassionate toward me like a friend. (540)
Having thus embraced Maheśāna, being impelled by the marriage ceremony, Sundara shall experience the auspiciousness of taking her hand in marriage. (Line 9) 541.
Thus, in the glorious Skanda Purāṇa, in the section on the Greatness of Śiva’s Devotees, [chapter] one...
Agastya:
...and likewise all the functions of the senses. 571.
They fell upon his face through the path of her two eyes;
she too, having observed the end of his gaze, recognized him, thinking, "This is he. (572)
For a moment he worshipped the beautiful one with garlands of side-long glances; for his eyes and her eyes met upon the path. (573)
Clinging tightly to one another, they both fell down, crushing those nearby.
Then, as she departed, Sundara,
whose mind was intent on the supreme mantra of the God of Love, followed her to the door of her neighbor's house.
Having taken that from his attendants while proclaiming his name, [he departed]. ||575||
With eyes closed in solitude, he contemplated that form: "Oh, what beautiful hair! Oh, how he gazes upon the earth with sidelong glances full of bewilderment! (576)
"Aha! My smile is a great moon for her face;
aha! Her pair of breasts is a great mountain range; aha! Her gait is exceedingly slow. As he thought thus, his mind became imbued with the very form of that slender maiden.
Having abandoned the five-syllable vidyā, one should take its four-syllable name. ||578||
As he was reciting, his mind became far removed from the blindness of lustful infatuation;
the chatter of the gardens became like the *kālakūṭa* poison to his ears. (579)
The wind from Mount Malaya became like the hissing of a serpent;
out of fear of seeing the moon upon [Śiva’s] crest, it did not serve the Lord of Tyāga. (580)
Dejected, he offered praise to the granter of boons to Mucukunda;
his body, motionless from grief, was as if smeared with ashes by the food [of sorrow], just as a son’s form might be covered in ash.
Having become Unmattaśekhara, he became a companion to Śambhu in that very place.
During the nights, the moonlight was like the fierce heat of the sun, while the sun’s rays were like the cool shade of the moon.
Even the act of reclining upon a bed of flowers became for him an entry into a heap of glowing coals;
his mind, withered by meditation and silence, was as if consumed by the fire of passion.
At night, as you were seated in sleep, Tyāgeśa spoke to Sundara:
"O Sukhasundara, while I am present, why do you go to the Daitya, leaving your grieving friend?"
"You do not praise me as you did before, nor is there pride or a smile upon your face; why is it that you sit in sleep, neither eating nor speaking? (585)
"O handsome one, tell me truly what illness has arisen within you;
for friends, having abandoned their grieving, find happiness only when they have comforted you.
Arise and tell me the cause of your sorrow; I shall pacify it."
O Sundara, this great mental anguish is difficult for you to ward off; for one who is without a protector, there is no bringer of peace.
I hear that you, the most excellent physician, are the friend who cures the disease of the bodiless god (Anaṅga).
There is a jewel among women named Sāgarikā, whose splendor is incomparable. ||588||
Taking that as their weapon, you torment me;
for her sake, I am consumed by the fever of love and endure great suffering. (589)
If her embrace could be obtained by me even once,
O Lord of Abandonment, this would undoubtedly be the fruit of my worship of you.
My mind, agitated by the thought of your form, dances about in the contemplation of your form.
Casting your auspicious name far away, I am devotedly intent upon the recitation of that other name.
(591) O Lord of Tyāgeśvara, ocean of compassion, grant this life-restoring medicine to the wretched messenger of desire, for the pacification of all mental anguish and physical disease. (592)
O Śaṅkara, if you go yourself as a messenger and bring her here, I shall offer ten thousand priceless lotuses to you, who are fond of praise. 593.
"O Master, if you disregard me even as I am being restrained by thousands of instructions on reality, then, while you look on, I shall give up my life. (594)
Having said "Agastya," the one who is affectionate toward his devotees addressed Sundara, who was prostrating at his feet;
having promised him "So be it," he assumed the form of a messenger. (595)
Then, at midnight, while all bodies were asleep,
the Lord of Renunciation appeared to the sleepless Sundara for the sake of quelling his suffering.
The sole dweller of all secret caves went to the abode of Sāgarikā;
as he went, that beautiful messenger was lovely with an application of camphor. (597)
Beholding the God who transcends the universe, the sky-dwellers were filled with wonder;
the streets were purified by the placement of his lotus feet.
Holding the King upon their heads, the Siddhas became liberated from their bonds. (598)
Or perhaps that Sāgarikā goes to Tyāgeśa acting as a messenger;
let the *kāhalī* trumpet resound in the sky, "Victory to the messenger Sundara!"—
for he departs in the form of a messenger without having spoken to Sundara’s friend.
The attendants informed the Queen of her divine majesty.
Seated upon the terrace of her jeweled palace, the mistress of the lotus-dwelling [Lakṣmī], beholding the Lord through the window, Gaurī wore a gentle smile. (561)

And the Goddess reflected in her mind that even this was an ornament for him, who dwells in cremation grounds, whose bed is the earth, and who bears the world like a bull—[an ornament] consisting of ashes, a garland of bones, and a skull-bowl.
(562) This mission as a messenger was for the sake of his friend; indeed, the diversion of the Lord of Beasts does not lead to any fault. (563)
Then Mahādeva, the treasure-house of compassion, passed beyond the great thoroughfare. ||563||
Sāgarikā went from her chamber to the doorway, which had an auspicious low railing,
where she touched that very stone slab— the lotus-foot of Paśupati— which the enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu), in his boar incarnation, had sought out like a swan. (564)

At night, even the nose and head [of the deity] assumed the form of a beautiful female messenger. (565) Then, having assumed the body of an attendant, Tyāgeśa, who possesses all forms, arrived at the gate for the purpose of opening it and spoke: "Who is here? (566)
Then, at midnight, having heard those profound words, she became apprehensive;
there, Sāgarikā remained sleepless along with Āryā.
"I shall see later, O Bālasāgarikā, what man [is this];
at midnight, having come to our house door, that woman is neighing.
Thus, with her hand placed upon the bolt, she stood there full of apprehension. (568)
There, Sundarāśayā spoke to her mother, Sāgarikā:
"O Mother, [this fragrance] is produced from camphor, jasmine, and Japā flowers. (569)
"Who is this drawing my nose outside? Let him be observed at the door!
Yesterday... [he] caused the creeper of his intellect to blossom, [a mind] daily adorned by the nail-marks and tooth-bites of Sāgarikā. (639)

Seeing his handsome friend rising to go— his body smeared with sandalwood paste from head to foot, radiant with a mouthful of betel-leaves crushed against his cheeks— he felt a joy equal to that of Lord Tyāgeśvara.
Then once, he approached him after he had performed his bath and completed his daily religious rites.
In his presence, the Lord of Renunciation spoke to him as he desired to offer praise:
"O friend, for you who have risen from the palace at dawn, Saudhārikā—"
O you whose mind is fixed on what is charming, always worship me. 642.
"Is there no work for me, the servant of my friend, that would bind [him]?"—
having been thus commanded by the Blessed One, Sundara served him accordingly.
In the millions of experiences of pleasure arising from his firm dalliances, consisting of smiles, glances, and amorous gestures, [Sundara’s] tender hands...
He did not forget his most trusted friend, Maheśa Tyāgeśvara, whose beautiful speech was praised by the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva).

Seeing the handsome Sundara sitting in his dwelling without having performed his daily rites, some remarked that he was a rogue attached to courtesans and thus unworthy of touch; others considered him to be Tyāgeśa, enriched by the grace of the Lord. (645) (6th line) Some people regarded him as Tyāgeśa, who is abundant in the favor of the Lord.
But Sundara, the friend of Śambhu, shall become equal to Nanda, who is worthy of praise.
For him who remembers Śiva, there is no fault in the enjoyment of courtesans,
just as there is no stain upon the current of the Gaṅgā from its contact with the earth that destroys karma.
Then one day, having seized him by the hand as he was returning from the morning [alms-round], the Lord of Āgā asked him privately: "O handsome one, where have you been? (648)
"O Sundarī, I ask you all: let the truth be spoken.
Let it be related how Sukhasāgarikā was seen in the company of Saṅgeya.
And as for that bliss from the touch of her jar-like breasts and from the firm embrace—"
That which is found in tasting the nectar of her lower lip, and that which is found in social gatherings with the fair-browed woman; ||650||
Out of friendship, O Lord, I ask you; such a question as this is not asked of anyone else.
You ought to tell me all of this exactly as it was experienced. (651)
O Śaṅkara, I know nothing at all of the enjoyer of delights and joys;
he knows no pleasure from the touch of bedding or fine garments.
They are the impellers of all the senses and dwell within the cave of the heart of every world.
"You alone are the doer and the enjoyer of this entire world, O Knower of the Ultimate Reality;
I am neither the doer nor the enjoyer, for I am merely one to be impelled by you. (654)
Whatever is seen or even heard in this world, every object whose nature consists of desire is composed entirely of you, O my [Lord]. (655)
Having spoken thus and prostrated at the lotus feet of Tyāgarāja, Sundara stood silently by his side like a servant beside his master. (656)
By his command, having praised the twice-born who dwell in the Tillakānana forest and being honored by them,
the wise one stood before their leader at the lake.
Observing the ripening of his mind, Maheśvara—
He bestowed the knowledge born of Vedānta, wherein this world appears like ripples upon water.

There sat Sanaka and the others, when the Lord of Sages had been bathed with the water from his own lotus feet and had been made successful by the initiation of knowledge, O beautiful one. (5th line) 659.
Having bowed down, Śaṅkara, the glorious one, while the sages were listening—even as they were engaged in their own duties—spoke these beautiful words concerning this doubt. (660)
The illustrious Maheśvara said:
"I am that which is actionless, stainless, peaceful, blameless, and untainted;
I am the perfect, inwardly directed light, the eternal reality. 661.
In the beginning, I alone was the infinite space; this world was neither other than me, nor non-existent, nor existent.
Then, when all things had dissolved, that which remained was I. 662.
O lords of sages, meditate with your minds upon me as a person the size of a thumb, dwelling in the cave of the heart, yet free from all latent desires, facing inward. 663.

The mind, impelled by Me, becomes the living being; the host of vital breaths (*asugaṇa*), urged by Me, moves within this [body], like water in a jar with holes—this is a marvel. (664) By which [mind] form is perceived, yet there is no perception of sound when it is damaged, because of the non-hearing of the word.
I am he who possesses a sweet-tasting tongue, and I am within all the senses.
In me, who am the light, the sun and other luminaries do not shine, nor do they act like lamps; rather, they all shine after me, just as an army follows its king. (666)
The elements born of the primary constituents are wiped away within me, like a transformation of water;
their differentiation from water is as false as the dream of Indra, or like the body [in sleep].
(667) While the elements are being perceived or dissolving within me...

This modification of mine is not ordained by fate; it arises from the union of the light [of consciousness] and the object. (668) Having realized, "I am that which is the uninterrupted knowledge extending from Brahma down to a blade of grass," the bound soul (paśu) is liberated from its fetters (pāśa). (669)

Two friends, birds dwelling upon this [tree], [drink] the cool streams of the *pippala* fruit; yet another, who shines forth among them, [is not like them]. These joys of action are but the spray of the ocean compared to me.
Having known this, the embodied being remains liberated from conceptual construction (saṅkalpa). ||671||
The sciences such as *anvīkṣikī* and the rest are not the causes of my realization; rather, O knower of that, the Upaniṣads alone illuminate me. (672)

Having known Me— who am to be known through the Upaniṣads— only through devotion after a long time by my grace, that ignorant person crosses over the insurmountable ocean of grief. (673) For whom neither the Nābhi nor the Lord creates or devours in that manner.
Having realized that [the Self] creates, sustains, and withdraws the world, one is liberated. ||674||
Having obtained refuge in me alone—the Supreme Lord dwelling in the hearts of all beings and the witness of all—they cross over [the ocean of existence], their purpose fulfilled. (675)
Thus, O Sundara, this knowledge born of the Vedānta has been imparted by me to you.
One who is dispassionate, having realized this, is liberated from the bonds of karma.
[676] (7th line) Through pure and supreme devotion, through austerity, and through the grace of the Guru—
Only a certain fortunate person, whose doubts have been resolved by direct perception, is liberated.
(677, 8th line) Therefore, O Sundara, you have come to me alone for refuge;
through my grace, you have obtained the Brahma-knowledge—be happy! (678)
Having recognized the form of all the Rudras, you shall not remember [anything] that is not luminous;
just as one who has cast off his slough does not look back upon it once he has departed.
Having meditated upon this seal of mine, which consists of pure consciousness, [you shall cross] to the other side of the ocean of births.
Having spoken thus and displaying the consciousness-constituted mudrā of Tyāgeśvara,
all of them— Sanaka and the others, as well as Sundara— their doubts completely severed and their minds fulfilled, prostrated themselves before Tyāgeśa a thousand times. (680–681)
Then, having been addressed by the Blessed One, Sanatkumāra and the others departed, constantly meditating upon the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā) shown by Tyāgeśvara. 682.

Sundara, seeking forgiveness from the Supreme Lord for his transgression against the messenger, attained supreme peace through the grace of the Destroyer of Smara, having become free from attachment to sense objects by means of a hundred hymns. (Agastya) 683. (2nd line) Agastya:

Those who hear and read this life-story of Sundara shall, by the grace of Śiva, attain liberation; of this there is no doubt. (684) [Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Śivabhaktamāhātmya* of the *Śrī Skandapurāṇa*.]
The *Sundaracarita* is completed. 685.
Agastya said:
There is no deity other than Mahādeva whose worship is so easily accomplished. In vain does the world serve other deities. (686)
Power exists for one's own liberation from the fear of time, and not for anyone else;
since Time is itself afraid, what will it accomplish by serving another?
(687) For those whose enjoyments are dependent on past karma, who perish again and again after having come into being—
The Blessed One, the Teacher of Time, is the sole one to be venerated by embodied beings. (688) But the fruit of his worship is exceedingly great: there is no further rebirth.
And his worship is easy to perform; it is only the fool who suffers in saṃsāra. (689)
Hara, the ocean of compassion, is pleased by unswerving devotion;
through His grace alone comes liberation, neither through knowledge nor through ritual action. (690)

For knowledge proceeds toward action only when there is a specific qualification (*adhikāra*). (8th line) The determination [of this] is made by the scripture: "All qualifications [arise] from devotion" (ŚBh 1.1.1). ||691||
