Śambhu is pleased when worshipped with devotion alone by a living being using leaves, flowers, fruits, and the like; he is gratified even by offerings of unworthy materials and so forth. (692) [He is also pleased] through yoga, by means of disciplined enumeration, and through austerity born of the highest birth.
By means of action, knowledge, and also devotion, thousands have been liberated.
On this very point, O Brahmins, I shall relate this narrative;
listen to it, for by the mere hearing of it, devotion to Śaṅkara arises. (694)
This supreme field is the ornament of this earthly realm;
by the mere sight of the glorious one named Cidambaram, liberation is granted to men.
(695) There, having witnessed the dance of the wielder of the Pināka bow within the golden assembly hall—
There were Vyāghrapāda and Patañjali, who had released the bonds of the tortoise [of worldly existence].
(696, 2nd line) There, in every house of the great-souled Brāhmaṇas, the purifying smoke arising from the *agnihotra* sacrifice rose both evening and morning. (697)
Shining forth, the fragrant smoke of the sacrificial cakes acts like a sprout of musk upon the faces of the women of the quarters. (698)
There lived a certain potter, the best of his clan, whose skill in crafting on earth was like that of Tvaṣṭṛ in heaven. He constantly bathed in the Śivagaṅgā and listened to the stories of Śiva.
He gave the ever-warming Bhaṇḍajāta for the delight of Nṛttarāja.
(700) He gives whatever is desired to the devotees of Śiva, being an excellent recipient;
contemplating the form of Śiva, he serves the devotees of Śiva. (701)
And his wife was an excellent chaste woman, preeminent in her devotion to Śiva. Despite being accompanied by her, that devotee had no son to perpetuate his lineage. (702)
And she would never experience distress on account of being childless,
for she was filled with the joy of devotion toward the glorious Lord of Citambara,
as she listened daily to the greatness of Śiva on the banks of the Śivagaṅgā. (703) (7th line)
The mind of Sakala was fixed upon the image of Naṭeśa. ||704||
Once, as he was remembering a portion of Śambhu’s power that had thrilled him in a dream, [the poison] reached the ear-lobe of Maheśa, which was radiant with the splendor of the Kālakūṭa. (705)
From that time forward, everyone always spoke of him with delight as "Nīlakaṇṭha";
indeed, he was given the name Nīlakaṇṭha by all the people. (706)
As he lived in this manner, a very great length of time passed by. Then, one day in the evening during the rainy season, [he beheld] a magnificent white lotus.
Having given [the gift] to Nṛttarāja, as he was returning toward his own home on the plateau,
there occurred a great rain accompanied by a massing of clouds.
By that [rain], the earth could not be discerned, much less the sky, the quarters, or what is above.
Afflicted by the downpour, his clothes were soaked and his mind was distressed. (709)
Then he went to the ground before the door of the courtesan’s dwelling. Recognizing him as Nīlakaṇṭha, the courtesan living there led him inside the house and kindled a fire with fuel.
Having given a dry garment and having offered betel and other items, ||711||
He bestowed the anointing of honor upon Śaika, who was about to depart;
yet, when the rain had ceased, Nīlakaṇṭha was not gladdened. (712)
Adorned with red ointment, he reached the house of the courtesan;
on the bed, regarding the application of his wife’s ointment...
[he] told her everything in truth, and her great suspicion was dispelled.
"For a long time you have been attached to courtesans; from this day forward, do not touch me. ||714||
"May the curse of the blue-throated one, who is praised by all, remain far away!"—thus addressed by the virtuous woman, he then replied with anger. (715)
Having heard from that worshipper, "I shall not touch you at all until the fall of my body," he [the king] again consoled him with words of pacification. (716)
Having made that promise, he too kept it within his heart.
While those two were thus dwelling together in constant quarrel, no one recognized that Maheśvara was the one causing it. (717)
Even though they are in close proximity to one another, it is due to the restraint of the senses. ||718||
Being well-pleased by his devotion, Naṭeśa granted him grace;
assuming the guise of a sage, Hara went to that dwelling.
(719) Rising and bowing to him, Nīlakaṇṭha then honored him.
Having offered him an excellent seat, the superior one asked, "What is to be done? (720)
Smiling, Maheśvara said to that blue-throated one:
"I, a yogin, have no desire for any invisible objects whatsoever. (721)
Nevertheless, O Nīlakaṇṭha, listen to a certain word from me:
this vessel [of a disciple] has been obtained by me through asceticism, one that is difficult for another to attain. (722)
Whatever I desire, you shall grant that to me;
protect this as a deposit until my return. (723)

Having said this and placed that food for the spirits into his hand, the sage Svairabhūti departed; and he, in turn, guarded it so that no one would know of the vessel and the mantra kept within the house. (724)
Having gone anywhere at all, he returns again without being wounded.

Those who guard the deposit of another, which is protected within the body by the movement of the vital breath like a treasure in a house, attain the eternal world. Having placed the bowl in the hand of that sage and having bestowed upon him the sense of having fulfilled his purpose, [he departed].
"Will he come? When will he come?"—thus he reflected.
(727) While he was thus absorbed in thought, that vessel created by Māyā vanished, just as a scripture disappears for one who fails to remember it. (728)
Then, having arrived, he was honored by the ascetic Nīlakaṇṭha:
"The protection of the region where the alms-bowl has been placed for you must be ensured;
there shall never be any doubt [regarding this]. May the Lord be gracious unto you."
"Give me that vessel of mine which protects me like a mother. (730)
Having bestowed food, ointments, garments, and whatever else was desired—O!—Nīlakaṇṭha, upon hearing that, established it in his house from every side. (731)
He did not see that bowl even though he searched for it again;
he asked his wife about the bowl, and she replied, "I do not know. (732) "Is this an illusion, or a nightmare, or a demonic possession? (7th line) "Or is it a delusion?"
O Nīlakaṇṭha, protect me from this censure of my intellect regarding the sacrifice.
"If I do not give up these vital breaths, she too will speak [the truth] regarding the non-existence [of the Dharma]," she thought in her mind and did not go into the presence of the Sage. (734)
Nīlakaṇṭha said to Patiśvaropita, "Let it be wept;
why is a delay being made now regarding my bowl? (735)
Then, terrified and with his mind bewildered by grief, he spoke to him:
"Listen to this; forgive me for this transgression. (736)
"That vessel of yours has been well-guarded by one of evil soul; behold it.
I give you another similar vessel; please accept it. (737) (Agastya)
While Nīlakaṇṭha was speaking thus, that great sage became enraged;
he summoned all those made of māṇikya and other gems and spoke as follows.
Oh, behold the misfortune of the evil-minded potter, who, having stolen a vessel that grants all desires, now wishes to give away a mere earthenware bowl! (2nd line) 739.
Your skill in deception is like that of the tiger Gomukha;
seeing you wearing ashes and rudrākṣa beads, I feel as though I have been deceived.
(740) [Third line] It is as if, having seized the cow, he now wishes to give away a donkey.
If some such conduct were to be recognized as approved in this world, ||741||
Constantly listening to the auspicious stories [of Śiva], adorned with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads,
he acted like a virtuous man toward others for the sake of seizing their property;
by taking from a child a divine object belonging to a twice-born man, he brought ruin to his family for seven generations.
Twenty-one [verses] were composed by Daheddhṛta for the deception of the clans. ||743||
The wealth taken from one who stands [in the lineage] would burn sixty-four families; that which is stolen from an ascetic (yati) certainly burns many millions of divine families. (744)
Therefore, I address you as Nīlakaṇṭha; let your hope cease.
Otherwise, you will surely fall into an abyss divided by millions of ancestral lineages.
Enduring that harsh speech, bow down with palms joined in reverence.
"I have not taken all the bowls," said the potter.
Then that sage spoke to Nīlakaṇṭha in the assembly of people:
"I have no confidence in your words; if they are true, then prove them. (747)
Having bathed in the waters of the Śivagaṅgā, touch your lineage [with water] from your head;
if you desire a wife, take her by the hand while wearing wet clothes.
Having bathed in the presence of Naṭeśa, utter this truth.
If that object is lost, then that vessel is destroyed; I am ruined along with my limbs.

Fearing the violation of his vow, that potter did not approve of the service at the feet of Naṭeśa by Nāryadhavalāsya, nor did he conceal all those riches of the sacrificers. (750) (9th line) Thus he feigned ignorance of all that.
When told, "The task must be done," he spoke what he had not heard before.
The Sage said, "Five shall not act in this manner," speaking thus with a threatening tone:
"If the cruel sage Nīlakaṇṭha stands as the witness for you two. (751-752)
"In this matter, a means has been seen; let this be heard by the members of the assembly.
Otherwise, we two shall fall from our feet upon reaching old age with our heads bent low.
(753) No calamities ever befall one who is devoted to Naṭeśvara," said the sage.
Let confidence be granted to that high-souled and majestic one. ||754||
What great men say when they have come together for the sake of welfare is indeed for the highest good;
for you two youths here have taken up two crores of bamboo staffs. (755)
Having heard these words spoken by Yajñasāhasra, "O Sage, having bathed in the waters of the Śivagaṅgā, [one is purified]," those two, the husband and wife,
grasped the tip of the sage’s bamboo staff and descended.
From that water of the Śivagaṅgā, as it was emerging, it took the form of a barley grain.
The two of them beheld the sage Naṭeśa mounted upon a bull;
the Blessed One, being pleased with them, granted them their desired liberation. (758)
Together with those two, he attained his own abode, the space of consciousness.
Whoever should read this chapter or listen to it with a concentrated mind—759.
"By the grace of Naṭeśvara, one is not born again on earth.

[Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Śivabhaktamāhātmya of the glorious Skandapurāṇa. (7th line) O sages, the life-story of the high-souled Sundara, who is identical with all beings, has been told.
Through devotion to Śaṅkhadatta, Maheśvara became his guru.
(761) Likewise, [the story] of Nīlakaṇṭha, who performed service to Śiva, and of the devotee Naṭeśvara whose life was heard [by you], has been recounted. (762)
Those who have no qualification for the means of attaining knowledge of the Vedānta, and who are themselves unable to perform service to the Enemy of Tripura; ||763||
Even those born of the Niṣkāula lineage desire liberation. By what means is he pleased so that he may grant them this liberation? Let that be told. (764) Agastya:
In this regard, listen to an ancient legend (itihāsa) as I recite it; by merely hearing it, one is liberated from the cycle of birth. ||765||
Thus, Śambhu is pleased by worship performed in accordance with their capacity, whether for men who are qualified for knowledge or those qualified for ritual action. (766)
Even for those born of low families whose natures are dull regarding knowledge and action,
the Lord delights embodied beings through the worship of His own devotees.
Whatever is most cherished in the world, when offered by a devotee of Śiva, [is pleasing to Him].
Even one who lacks the transmission of those respective [teachings] is immediately liberated by virtue of his birth. ||768||
In this world of mortals, there are many who, through their singular devotion to Śiva and their offspring, have been instantly liberated from bondage by the grace of Śambhu. ||769||

Just as the Lord who bears the moon upon his crest gladdens all beings through the practice of medicinal treatments, sacrifices, rituals, austerities, vows, gifts, and the well-performed mantras, tantras, nigamas, and āgamas, so too does he [gladden] those devoted to his own feet through their devotion. (770)
In the southwestern quarter, there is a city adorning the banks of the Kāverī,
a treasury for the wealthy in this world and a multiplier of riches for merchants;
where even a person of little merit becomes destitute by residing there for only a single year.
Having attained great prosperity, he now prospers even through the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
When the nine treasures had been carried off by the inhabitants of that place, the great ocean, raising its waves like hands, cried out day after day. (773)
Not far from there lived a certain man named Nada, who was of equal fortune [to himself],
renowned for great wealth, and highly skilled in the examination of jewels. Even a small amount of wealth, once touched by his hand, would increase.
All his kinsmen, who were followers of the path of the subtle, became his servants.
In his childhood, he was seen endowed with [such splendor] that he appeared like another Mount Meru;
the earth became possessed of all its auspicious characteristics. ||776||
He had millions of kinsmen by whom the world was surrounded;

he enjoyed pleasures difficult even for the gods to obtain—enjoyments consisting of houses, ornaments, ointments, and garments, blazing with intense splendor. (777) (P.31b, F.30a, 1st line) Ugrajvala.

Thus, for him who was accompanied by his wife, a great period of time passed. (2nd line) (…) His son, whose hand was not [useless] (…) was always with his wife; with a weary mind, he had cast off his ornaments. 779.
Having appointed one servant to look after the house, he lived there in silence;
but once, having bathed at dawn along with his wife,
he desired to go to Guha’s dwelling on the bank, as the Purāṇas declare.
Thus addressed by Satya, he, together with his wife, listened to the story.
Therefore, from hearing the Śiva-purāṇas recited by the most excellent of Brahmins, his devotion to Śiva arose through the merit of those stories of Śiva. (782)

Day after day, the mind of that detached man, together with his wife, was intent upon listening to the Purāṇa; thus, their latent desire for sense-objects became pacified. Those two, the husband and wife, [served] the aged brahmin who was firmly established in the principles of Śiva.
Having given to him the unsurpassed five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣara), which is the tortoise-mantra that bestows grace,
as well as the sacred field, clothing, and the planets and limbs, the man of purified intellect became one who was deeply devoted to the Purāṇas of Sadāśiva and possessed great wealth. ||784–785||
Bowing humbly with palms joined in reverence, he asked:
"O Lord, how may liberation be attained by me, a seeker of release, through your grace? (786)
Whether through knowledge or through action performed according to the prescribed rules,
Maheśvara, the creator of the world, is propitiated when worshipped. (787) Since I have no authority over those two, how will liberation come to pass?
The ancients praise ancient traditions; knowledge of action is supreme.
“If you are omniscient, O treasury of compassion, please purify this doubt of mine.
Having heard these words of his disciple, the Guru spoke:
“If you have faith in my words, then [be gracious] toward Maheśvara…”
But one who is of a doubting nature regarding the words of others perishes. ||790||
Having completely abandoned attachment to the unreal, always cultivate association with the real and the unreal.
Listen also to the characteristics of the unreal; I shall describe them. (791)
(…) Through mere knowledge, one becomes associated with the flow of the intellect;

yet, those characterized by the marks of the virtuous remain attached to worldly conventions, their minds preoccupied with the doctrine that the body is the self and possessing desire for the fields of existence. 792.
But for those who possess Vaiśya-sorrow, it is difficult to overcome. ||793||
Those for whom the company of the virtuous is esteemed dwell in conversation with the wise;
now hear from me as I describe the characteristics of the good. (794)
Śiva alone is the creator of the world; in Śiva everything is established.
He is the one who, together with the sun, shows the path to those wandering in the darkness of karma.
He alone is the refuge; there is no other deity to be sought.
"O Lord of Śivā and Gaurī, O Śambhu, victory to you, O wearer of the crescent moon!
(796, 5th line) Protect me, who am like a morsel for Time, O Kālaśāsana, O Śaṅkara!"—
those of firm vows who thus proclaim the names of Śiva, (797)

For those devoted to the worship of the Śiva-liṅga and wearing sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, may there be liberation even from sin; yet that [liberation] is incomplete without service at his feet. (798)
O people, by giving to the Supreme Lord whatever is most dear to those devotees, one quickly becomes a recipient of Śiva’s grace;
likewise, for those who perform the worship of his own feet, he is swiftly pleased. (799)
Just as Śambhu follows and is pleased by the worship of his devotee. ||800||
By performing this, a person delights the devotees of Śiva in the world; through the grace of Śiva, he crosses over the difficult-to-traverse sorrow of saṃsāra. 801.
"By serving the feet of a Śiva-devotee and offering him desired garments,
[one attains this] even without the exertion of practicing for knowledge. (9th line) Having been thus instructed by his own guru, he bowed to him and said, "So be it."
He was fortunate, for he performed service at the feet of the devotees of Śiva. ||803||
He prostrates hundreds of times to the one whose hair is marked with ashes and then asks about his desired object. ||804||
He grants without delay that which is desired and difficult to obtain;
with all his limbs smeared with ashes and wearing a garland of rudrākṣa beads...
(805, second line) He should be a constant giver of food to his devotees and eat their leftovers.
And his wife was devoted to her husband, her devotion following whatever he desired. ||806||
Neither his kinsmen nor his actions approved of that deed of his, which was contrary to what should be done for one's teachers and inconsistent with their words. ||807||
They offered their opposition, yet he did not heed their words:
"This servant, who eats the remnants of others, is desired by those who smear themselves with ashes;
for, being devoted to praising his enemies, he performs only what is improper. (808)
"Thus, though summoned by my own kinsmen, I did not waver from my own duty.
'I am not a devotee of Śiva, nor am I one who would worship him when he is not honored'—thus, O Lord, a great period of time passed for me, your servant and devotee. (809–810)
Having bestowed everything he had earned as grain upon the Brahmins, the Lord of Umā became pleased with him who subsisted on a portion of that food. (811)
At midday, a twenty-five-year-old pseudo-Brahmin, Vidhāya, arrived at the door of that house wearing his [ascetic] garb;
marked with eight lines of ash, he cried out loudly, "Give me alms! (812)
Taking that grain and food, his wife went outside.
Beholding her, that twice-born man, the crest-jewel of the rogues of the earth, stood still;
though told, "Accept alms," he did not accept them at all. ||814||
As he stood there, his gaze fell upon her face;
seeing that look, the virtuous woman became apprehensive and said, "O Lord, it is I.
(815) Having received that alms-food... [hear... (9th line).
Mahādeva, laughing, spoke thus to the rogue:
(816) “I have come for the sake of alms-food; food is obtained at every house.
Grant me the desired object of this twice-born man; give me alms…” (817)
Then, having bowed to that merchant, [he said: "Alms are being given;
if they are granted, I shall speak, otherwise I shall depart as I came. (818)
"Let there be no delay," said the Brahmin;
having spoken thus, he bowed at his feet with palms joined in reverence.
Then the young woman requested alms from the learned twice-born man, who was free from all doubt.
Without further deliberation, he whose mind was fixed on Śiva gave her away there along with his wife. ||820||
Then, urged by her husband, she approached the brahmin with palms joined in reverence;
meanwhile, her enraged kinsmen rose up to slay the brahmin. But that compassionate hero, sword in hand, restrained his relatives and said, "Do not kill him. (821)

Having slain his kinsmen who were hostile to his own dharma, as he looked about, he did not see a single Brāhmaṇa; then, filled with wonder, he questioned his wife. When she replied, "I do not know," he remembered Śaṅkara in his heart. (822-823)
Maheśvara was seen mounted upon his bull together with Gaurī, being praised by hosts of gods and accompanied by his attendants bearing musical instruments. 824.
Having granted liberation to the Vaiśya couple— longed for by the hosts of sages—
he beheld them established among the Siddhas and returned to his own abode. (825) What is the use of manifold and difficult rituals, or of knowledge so hard to attain through many births?
The Supreme Lord Maheśa is pleased by devotion; therefore, having cast aside all other things, one should be devoted to Him.
[Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Śivabhaktamāhātmya of the glorious Skandapurāṇa.]
O twice-born ones, Agastya [declared that] the merit of daily providing water for the consumption of Śiva’s devotees becomes a source of pleasure for Śambhu in this world. (828)
The city of Kaniṣkagila is the ornament of the earth,
always filled with Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas devoted to their own duties,
as well as Śūdras intent upon serving the twice-born. (829)
It was filled with devotees of Śiva who were devoted to the observance of Śiva’s vows. ||830||
There was a certain person known as Māra, born of low caste; the Lord, being pleased by the service rendered at the feet of Śiva-devotees who were Śūdras, [granted him his desire]. ||831||
Thus, with a mind made steady by the teacher’s instruction and through constant charity, he should worship those devoted to Śiva.
His wealth, acquired by righteous means, increased like the ocean.
He joyfully employed all of that for the sake of worshiping [the deity] with food offerings. ||833||
From the rising of the sun until the break of dawn, day after day, he gives the four kinds of desired food to the devotees of Śiva. (834)
After testing his devotion, Maheśvara [resolved] upon the mind of that sonless man who, together with his wife, was a provider of food to his devotees;
and by the command of the Lord of All, [He took] his entire collection of wealth.
Day by day it reached decline, like the moon in the dark fortnight. ||836||
Although Māra’s wealth was exhausted, with his mind as focused as before, he gave food to those who arrived by selling his fields, vessels, and other possessions. (837)
When the household utensils had thus been exhausted through the giving of food,
only his wife remained, along with the auspicious thread on her neck.
Then, on a certain day during the rainy season, when the sky was shrouded in darkness—
At midnight, a certain ascetic, tormented by hunger and thirst, [arrived]. ||839||
Having searched and sought him out, he slowly approached the house of Māra;
having arrived at the door of that house, he assumed the form of a mendicant through his illusory power. (840)
Having summoned Māra, the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, said this:
"I am hungry and thirsty; I am exhausted from my ascetic penance and unable to speak.
Having heard from afar that you provide food, I have come to your house. (841)
Give to me, who am afflicted by hunger and have arrived here. ||842||
"Furthermore, for ascetics, the father and mother are the givers of food.
Having heard this statement, he departed together with his wife;
having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, he offered water for the feet and a seat.
He who did not look upon [it] with joy... ||844||
Having thus spoken, she softly said this to the housewife:
"Come, O virtuous lady; at this very hour of night, a great ascetic has arrived. (845)
“‘Give food to one who is hungry’—thus he begs, and his mind suffers.
I find no means here by which his hunger might be appeased.
This birth would be in vain if he were to fast here. (846) (3rd line)
"O Māyāvin, no one on earth is as wretched as I am. (847)
When an ascetic, having entered my house, rises up with a sneeze, he seeks refuge in the household as his husband seeks the supreme goal. (848)
He who has not obtained a compliant wife must go to the forest;
yet she, being both compliant and virtuous, was turned into leather by her beloved.
(5th line) By virtue of your compliance, I am the giver of food to my devotees.
O you who are devoted to your husband, you alone are my refuge here; deliver me! (850)
Having heard these words of her husband, the wife said to her lord:
"O Lord, I see no means whatsoever here for you to enter the house. (851)
This handful of salt was left behind by me during the day;
I have not eaten and shall not stay here without it, O Lord, for I have seen a means [to obtain it].
(852) The various seeds sown in the field yesterday are not far away.
"We have [this]; do not fall into despondency—let this be employed. ||853||
"Let that be brought by you; I shall prepare it myself. (8th line) Mung beans have been sown and have sprouted on the courtyard of your house. (854)
"By the grace of Mahādeva, there is nothing lacking here whatsoever.
Hearing these words of his wife, the ascetic spoke joyfully: "Māra, sleep here for a moment; [your master] is being cooked. (856) (9th line)
"By good fortune you have arrived at midnight; I am fulfilled by the mere sight of you. (857)
Having heard these words of Māra, he entered into the practice of asceticism;
even though it was practiced, he illustrated [the futility of it] by citing the example of seeds sown in barren soil. (858)
At that very moment, the virtuous woman prepared a vegetable dish for herself using the remaining leaves of the mudga beans and salt;
she also gathered seeds with their sprouts and carried them away.
She said that her husband was not to be attained [by her], and that he should be awakened through asceticism. ||860||
Even Māra, along with his friends, intent on awakening the ascetic, arrived; exhausted, he said, "Please accept this offering. (861)
Speaking thus, he reached his presence and beheld the god who partakes of the oblations,
mounted upon his bull, marked by the seal of fearlessness,
and embraced by Gaurī as she rests upon his left side. (862)
Bowing down many times in fear, he went for refuge at his feet. ||863||
And his wife, with a joyful heart, presented the offering to him; the sages, praising me with their words, rained down showers of flowers upon my back. (864)
All the hosts played various musical instruments;
then the blessed Lord Īśvara, the husband of Ambikā, became pleased. (6th line) 865.
Having granted liberation to these two, he vanished along with them.
[Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Śrī Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Māhātmya of Śiva’s Devotees*. (866) Agastya:
Those who, though constantly worshipping devotees possessing the three states of Śiva, forgive the transgressions of those who wear ashes and rudrākṣas;
and when a doubt arises among Brahmins, those who desire to attain the favor of Śiva— [these are the ones who should be honored]. (867) (8th line)
For they are indeed vessels of Śiva’s grace, being free from any act of hostility. ||868||
Those who honor even those devotees who have personally committed an offense—Śiva is pleased with them more than by ten million sacrifices. (869)
(…) O Brahmins, listen to that which is renowned,
by the mere hearing of which we may become firm in devotion to Śambhu.
(870) In the land of Cedi, there is a certain supreme place presided over by cowherds.
Truth is the most excellent among these worlds... ||871||
They constantly bestow what is desired upon the devotees of Śiva;
when requested by a devotee of Śiva, they even give up their own lives. ||872||
Seeing that, the lord of the mandala was distressed:

"There is cessation [of suffering] for those devoted to Śiva; I am not such a one, nor do I belong to anyone. While he was thus situated, the Lord of Liberation, the King, [appeared]. 873. (3rd line) To him who was so disposed, the Lord of Liberation, the Sovereign of the Earth...
The enemy of existence becomes his foe, and his foot becomes like a thief. ||874||
Having utterly defeated that powerful enemy in battle,
the king seized his army, wealth, and entire city by force.
Muktinātha, being weak, was cast out from the field by him alone.

Having lost all his possessions, he fled and hid somewhere within the depths of the forest. (876) Waiting for the arrival of the appointed time and looking for a flaw in the enemy’s month, he reached a stratagem and, having deliberated thus by himself, (877) [acted].
Having entered the city of Kāravaṇī as an ascetic carrying a book, he, smeared with ashes, went to the gate of Satyabhāmā’s residence. (878)
Then her husband lay down, overcome by sleep from hunting;
while his enemy, disguised in the dress of an ascetic, watched for the end. (879) While the king was sleeping, [the enemy thought: "What business have you with me? Stay either inside or outside."
Although restrained by the doorkeepers, that ascetic did not cease from looking at them. ||880||

Having forcibly compelled [the king] with the words, "Go," in order to instruct the lord of the earth in the true meaning of the secret scriptures (*rahasyāgama-tattvārtha*), he went to the house of his enemy’s bedchamber. 881.
Having observed the ascetic approaching, bearing a book and with a mass of matted hair rising high, Rāma’s husband should awaken him. And he,
being awakened, [recognizes] the enemy by means of his true purpose concealed by a disguise.
Not knowing [the reason for his arrival], O great ascetic, he prostrated himself out of fear; (P.35b, F.34a, 1st line) (…) he said: (…) “Do not sit me upon a high seat.
I am blessed, I am graced by the sight of your lotus-feet. (884)
This life has been consecrated by the dust from the feet of my gurus;
through service to you, this mind of mine now becomes serene. (885)
What should I do? What should be performed? Command me and show me favor. O Master, my power extends not only over wealth and such things;
truly, those like you have authority even over my very life.
While the king was speaking thus, [the two of them] folded their hands in a gesture of humility.
He spoke with a smiling face that concealed his ascetic nature:
"Listen, O Indra among kings, to my words; for you are the foremost among devotees. (888)
"O King, we have come to awaken you to the secret meaning of the principles of Śiva;
listen to this alone, O ruler of truth!
And this scripture was described by the Lord to Gaurī on Kailāsa."
Having heard this, the king said to his wife, "Go outside. ||890||
And when she had gone outside, he did not cover his face with the door-panel;
having given him ashes, the ascetic said to him, "I have heard that [you say] 'namas' to him. (891)
Saying "So be it," he rose and, while the lord of the earth was bowing at his feet,
struck him in the vital spot of his own vehicle with a concealed sword from its scabbard.
Struck by the blow of the sword, he fainted;
crying out, "Alas, I am slain!", he stood distressed and rushed forward in anger.
Having burst through the door with speed, he seized the ascetic by the hand.
He struck Jaṭā... with that very sword in order to kill him. ||894||
In an instant, King Satyārtha opened his eyes and, seeing the guards standing there, commanded them:
"You are bound by oath upon my life; do not kill him! (9th line) || 895 ||
Having formed a compact, the brave warriors, though enraged,
remained restrained by their oath to their lord, even while filled with fury.
That king, enduring their blows, said to him, "Do not fear."
Having meditated upon him trembling, disguised by his attire... ||897||
People led him away from the object [of his offense], saying, "How can you overlook an enemy who has committed an injury against you? Thus was he questioned by the assembly of people. (898)

"Even though he has committed an offense against me and is smeared with the ashes of my enemies, he is indeed my lord; I bear no enmity toward him," he spoke. (899) Having heard from the mouth of the messenger that the ascetic was well, the king—
He highly esteemed his own soldiers, who were observers of the sacrificial rites.
The supreme king Satyārtha, with a mind [fixed on] the center,
attained liberation even while in the presence of Maheśa, O lord of the earth.
(901) Though carried away by his devotees, though moistened by their words of consolation, and though brought back to life—
He who spreads what is beneficial for the pleasure of Śiva, the moon-crested Lord.
To him, being pleased, they grant that he shall no longer suffer the pain of rebirth.
[Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Śivabhaktamāhātmya of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.]
Devotion to the lotus feet of Sadāśiva is supremely purifying;
it is obtained here by the fortunate through merits accumulated in previous births. (904)
By means of this, O Lord of the destruction of the fear of existence, may this embodied being cross the difficult-to-traverse ocean of saṃsāra,
with the cage of the tiger-like bonds of existence utterly severed.
(905) Just as devotion to Śiva is the primary means for liberation, [so too is this].
And devotion to the feet of a devotee of Śiva is likewise the sole means to liberation. ||906||
Śaṅkara accepts worship directly in the form of devotion;
when worshipped in lingas and other such forms, he accepts it only indirectly. (907)
They praise the service at the feet of devotees who possess the manifest form of God; they do not praise a servant of the Lord who is beyond perception.
For those [devotees], through seeing, association, conversation, and service at the feet... [he attains liberation].
For those grieving here in this saṃsāra, their sorrow is instantly dissolved.
(909) Without [the service of] her feet, and without reflection upon the Vedānta, who in this world could be liberated along with [their kin] through service to the lotus-feet of the Devotee? (90)
(…) Where the devotion of a devotee is thus described:
there exists in the region of Kerala a city named Śoṇācala.
There, among his devotees, there arose a great deal of talk regarding cessation [of worldly activity];
yet their devotion toward the Supreme Lord was not so great. (913)
As he was conducting himself in this manner, [his] mind [...
(4th line). Whatever man, having committed an offense against Śiva or a devotee of Śiva, should kill that sinner with this [weapon], [his] life [... (5th line).
(…) He stands on the great path, the most delightful and supreme, carrying his devotees who come along the way. 916.
He honored [the hero] in the mind of Vīra Indra. ||917||
A certain thought arose in his mind: "Those on earth who are devoted to the Moon (Candra) [and yet] do not serve [him]—the birth of such beings is in vain, for they have not beheld him.
Having circumambulated the earth and having wandered [over it]..."
This human birth has been attained through the company of the virtuous. ||920||
Thus, while the descendant of Bhṛgu remained established in his vow, [the two of them] were drawn away from their domain; that field became renowned throughout the three worlds,
where the Lord who bestows liberation grants the body’s release.
(…) Indeed, that pair of herons departed from there slowly toward the abode of Lakṣmī (the lotus).
Having given a great [gift] there, he... (2nd line)
Then, having conquered anger, he fulfilled the desires of those devoted to him within his own abode. ||925||
To those whose bodies were smeared with ashes and adorned with rudrākṣas, who were intent on initiation and devoted to the Śiva-vow,
and who were listeners of the Śiva-purāṇas and [worshippers] of the Śiva-liṅga...
With his body covered in horripilation from devotion, he bowed down before those virtuous ones. ||928||
He also made this known:
“I am one who acts with the power to suppress those who harm the devotees of Śiva;
grant me permission to always [be] present.”
(…) as long as he continues to worship his devotees and the Brahmins with the contemplation of the Lord. ||931||
...in the service of the Supreme Lord. ||932||
Even having abandoned that, they indeed remain bearers of the burden of Śiva’s work;
in this [matter] … (8th line) … the bundle of betel leaves is characterized by the smoke of the sacrificial fire.
Enveloped by fine garments stained with the cosmetics of a courtesan, he [attained me], Maheśvara, after serving me for many [lifetimes]. (934–935)
Disregarding and not looking at these [men], Vīrami...
||936|| ...the hero Indrasaśya, becoming enraged, took up his axe to slay that [attacker]...
||937|| Seeing the assailant approaching, Sundarī was struck with fear.
(…) in his presence, Sundara sought refuge with his friend, the Lord of Renunciation. ||938||
